Observed facts: the patient received bilateral total knee arthroplasties, then 19 months later a single intravesical BCG instillation followed by mitomycin. Sixteen months after BCG he developed bilateral knee pain, worse on the left, without systemic symptoms. Examination showed mild warmth and effusions; vital signs were stable. Inflammatory markers were modestly raised (ESR 32 mm/h, CRP 1.6 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.1 ng/mL) with normal blood count and liver tests. Imaging did not show loosening or overt infection. Right‑knee aspirate Gram stain and routine cultures were negative; synovial cell count and chemistry are unavailable. Acid‑fast stain was negative, but delayed mycobacterial culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Strain identification and outcome data are pending.

Hypotheses: the isolate may represent BCG‑derived Mycobacterium bovis, a reactivated Mycobacterium tuberculosis, or a laboratory contaminant. The long latency after BCG and the bilateral involvement raise the possibility of haematogenous seeding of both prostheses.

Proposed actions before any management decision: (1) request definitive speciation (e.g., PCR, whole‑genome sequencing) and drug‑susceptibility testing of the isolate; (2) obtain left‑knee aspiration for cell count, chemistry, acid‑fast stain, culture and mycobacterial PCR; (3) refer to an infectious‑diseases physician and a revision arthroplasty surgeon for joint assessment; (4) evaluate for disseminated disease (chest imaging, HIV test, interferon‑gamma release assay). These steps will clarify the organism, its resistance pattern, and the extent of infection, allowing a tailored therapeutic and surgical plan.
